title: Pete Edochie: How Nigeria's Things Fall Apart star became a Nollywood legend
description: For generations of Nigerians, Pete Edochie was more than a celebrated actor. He was Okonkwo – the fierce, proud and troubled warrior whose portrayal i
body: For generations of Nigerians, Pete Edochie was more than a celebrated actor. He was Okonkwo – the fierce, proud and troubled warrior whose portrayal in Things Fall Apart made him a household name and earned him a place in the hearts of millions.Even in death, many Nigerians still refer to him by the character's name, a testament to the enduring impact of a role that defined his career.Edochie died on 25 November, aged 79, in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.In 1987, Edochie starred in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel. His portrayal of Okonkwo would change his life, establishing him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors and bringing him international recognition.The series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.Joy Nnamdi, a fan of both the novel and its television adaptation, believes Edochie was the perfect choice for the lead role.She said nobody else could have brought the character to life as convincingly."His character Okonkwo gave a face to the highly celebrated novel," she told the BBC in Nigeria's biggest city, Lagos.The role also cemented his reputation as a hard man, a screen persona he would maintain through much of his career."It was very rare to see him laugh in movies. He was the ultimate tough man," Nnamdi added.With his deep, authoritative voice, imposing presence and effortless command of African proverbs, Edochie had a way of dominating a scene without raising his voice.Whether playing a village elder, a wealthy businessman or a feared traditional ruler, he became an enduring embodiment of patriarchal authority on screen.Edochie went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has grown into one of the world's largest.From Kenya to South Africa, MultiChoice's Africa Magic channels helped take his films into millions of African homes as Nollywood became a cultural phenomenon across the continent.Although many of his films were rooted in his Igbo culture, their themes of family loyalty, inheritance disputes, spiritual beliefs and the abuse of power resonated with audiences far beyond Nigeria.Before becoming a household name in the film industry, however, Edochie had built a successful career in broadcasting.Born on 7 March 1947 in Zaria, northern Nigeria, he attended primary and secondary school in Kaduna before studying journalism and television at the School of Journalism and Television in the UK.He joined the Eastern Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation in 1967, the year Nigeria's civil war broke out.He joined the pro-separatist Voice of Biafra, and recently described the war years as the greatest personal challenge he ever faced."During the war, the experience that we had as Biafrans, you know, survival was difficult. Hunger was driving us into eating all sorts of nonsense," he recalled.He rose through the ranks to hold senior management positions but then switched to acting. Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals and Billionaire's Club. His career also bridged the transition from home-video productions to global streaming platforms. The 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart, which became Netflix's first original Nigerian film, introduced his work to a wider international audience.He also worked in Ghana, where he starred alongside some of the country's biggest film stars in the 2017 comedy John and John.His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).He also received several other accolades, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.In recent years, Edochie found an unexpected new audience online.His distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films became popular social media memes, introducing his work to a younger generation of Africans.For many who had never watched Things Fall Apart or his early Nollywood films, his stern expressions became a humorous way of conveying disbelief, disapproval or exasperation at everyday situations.But his reputation as a formidable screen presence was no joke to those who grew up watching him.Sani Muazu recalls that parents in the northern Nigerian city of Kano would sometimes invoke Edochie's name to keep misbehaving children in check."They would tell you: 'Okonkwo will come and visit you if you don't stop' and we would begin acting right," he said."To be honest, we grew up scared of him. Even though he was on the screen and not physically present, some of his roles added to our fears because he played some popular occultic roles, and villain roles suited him."Tributes poured in from fans and fellow actors following news of his death, with many describing him as a giant who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.Popular actress Genevieve Nnaji paid her tribute in a post on X."I will let the assurance of the fact that you are a chosen one; and therefore, have returned to the most high God override my grief and heartbreak. May the heart of a true lion forever rest in peace. We love you," she wrote.Patience Ozokwor, popularly known as Mama G, who appeared alongside Edochie in several productions, remembered him as a brilliant actor and a source of wisdom."He has been a father to stories that are told, like an elder sitting down telling you how things were done in those days," she told BBC News Pidgin."I called him any time, any day. He'll tell you what to do and what not to do."Film director Babangida Bangis told the BBC that Edochie's death was a loss not just for Nigeria or Africa, but for the global film industry."Just days ago, during a seminar for filmmakers across the country, his name popped up as an example of brilliance on the screen, longevity and professionalism," he said."I think his loss is one for the world, not just Nigeria or Africa. We all grew up watching and loving him."Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu also mourned the veteran actor, describing his death as a major loss to the country's film industry and cultural heritage.The president, like many admirers, singled out Edochie's portrayal of Okonkwo, saying the performance and his subsequent roles had established him as one of Nigeria's most accomplished actors.But beyond the fame and formidable character he portrayed on screen, his family remembers a man whose greatest legacy was the importance he placed on honesty and speaking the truth.Leo Edochie, his son, told the BBC that his father was a strong-willed man."Of all his legacies, I think the whole world would agree that these two were the most important: telling the truth and remaining honest," he said.He described his father as a man who lived an exemplary life, offering a model that young people could learn from and aspire to follow."I don't really have a choice, but the truth is that I have to carry on that legacy for our family," he added.Edochie's influence also extended to his family, with two of his six children, Yul and Linc Edochie, following him into the Nigerian film industry.Yet, for an actor so closely associated with stern expressions and intimidating characters, some of his most endearing moments came when he let his guard down.In 2021, he made a brief appearance in music star Phyno's video for the song Highway, surprising fans with a display of dance moves that showed a lighter, more playful side of the septuagenarian.It was a refreshing reminder that the man behind the formidable screen persona could also laugh, dance and enjoy himself.
